title: If Labor was ever minded to revise AUKUS, it has already passed up two golden opportunities, writes Sam Roggeveen.
text:

ANALYSIS: As the US downgrades the nuclear submarines deal to second-hand vessels, Australia’s options to back out have narrowed to one possible shift in domestic politics.

Australia’s future Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarines will all be second-hand – it’s about simplicity, according to Defence Minister Richard Marles. Previously, one of the boats was going to come fresh from the American production line but now all will be transferred from United States Navy service. Virginia-class submarines are built in versions or “blocks” so that new technology and design features can be incorporated over time. Australia will now get one block rather than two.

“What we will have here is a simpler pathway,” Marles told reporters at the International Institute for Strategic Studies Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore last week. “The Virginias we are acquiring will all be of the same type and I can’t overstate the significance of that.”

Of course, one easily could overstate the significance of this change, as the deputy prime minister went on to demonstrate by acknowledging it won’t make much difference to the price Australia pays for its submarines.

Still, Marles had a point. Before this latest announcement, Australia was effectively proposing to conduct four overlapping submarine projects: the upgrade of the navy’s existing Collins-class boats; introducing two versions of the Virginia-class; and the design and construction of an all-new submarine to be built in the United Kingdom and Adelaide. That’s now back to three, which, given Australia has never managed more than one submarine project at a time, still leaves plenty of room for risk.

Shadow defence minister Senator James Paterson had an uncomfortable question for the government: if getting only second-hand submarines is so clearly the right decision, why wasn’t it taken at the outset? Something else had clearly changed, but what?

The most plausible answer is that the US wants to keep the newest and most advanced version of the Virginia for itself. American shipyards are struggling to raise their productivity enough to fill the US Navy’s own order books, let alone meet the commitment to Australia. So the Pentagon is cutting its cloth, with Marles left to make the best of it.

The announcement reinforced a sense of scepticism about whether the Virginia-class submarines can be delivered at all. Up to this point, questioning of AUKUS has come predominantly from the progressive side of Australian politics. According to a report in The Australian newspaper this week, that now includes Labor Party backbencher Ed Husic and sections of the union movement.

Concerns about AUKUS now appear to be gaining purchase on the right, too. The Liberal Party had hitherto been loath to even consider the possibility of delays, but Senator Paterson gave a speech in April calling for the government to investigate alternative weapon systems that “may help fill any capability gaps that arise”.

If Labor was ever minded to revise AUKUS, it has already passed up two golden opportunities ... We may now have come too far to go back.

Former Abbott government treasurer Joe Hockey was more direct. Hockey is well briefed on this topic, as founding partner of the Washington, DC-based consultancy Bondi Partners, which says on its website: “With the evolution of AUKUS … Bondi Partners footprint continues to grow across the Pacific and the Atlantic.”

Hockey recently told the National Press Club that, for the first time, he was “a little nervous” about the delivery schedule for the Virginia-class submarines.

It raises a question that has seemed implausible until now: could the Albanese government step away from the AUKUS submarines? Is there a realistic pathway towards cancellation?

There are strong reasons to believe the government will maintain its commitment. For one thing, Marles is a powerful figure in the cabinet and appears to sincerely believe in the project.

If Labor was ever minded to revise AUKUS, it has already passed up two golden opportunities. It could have come to office in 2022 announcing an inquiry on the entirely justifiable basis that its endorsement of the project while in opposition was based on very little information released by the Morrison government.

Failing that, the Albanese government could have used the opportunity created by the Pentagon’s decision to review AUKUS, announced in June last year. That would have been the perfect moment to quietly communicate to the Trump administration that, if the review should happen to recommend against proceeding, Australia wouldn’t be too upset. This would have avoided any need for the government to take a “courageous” political stand against AUKUS. The prime minister could have told the nation this was America’s decision and, regretfully, Australia would have to move on from a flawed Morrison government initiative.

We may now have come too far to go back. Governments that invest significant political and financial capital in a major project are typically reluctant to admit a mistake, though it can happen. The last budget saw the cancellation of Inland Rail, which was expected to balloon to $45 billion. And, of course, Australia cancelled the French Attack-class project in 2021 to embark on AUKUS. But Australia had invested a mere $4 billion in the Attack-class before it was terminated; the sum for AUKUS is already more than twice that figure.

You might identify this as a textbook example of the sunk cost fallacy, a cognitive bias that sees people continue to pursue a project simply because they have already invested time, money and effort into it, even though it would be in their interest to stop. It’s not yet clear enough that AUKUS is failing for the government to think in these terms. AUKUS is inordinately risky, but we are still in the foothills of a project that will take 30 years or more, and it can’t be said that project is presently in crisis.

Another argument is that Australia has spent so long dithering over submarines that if we back out of AUKUS now, it will be too late to find submarines elsewhere before the Collins boats are retired. Australia, it is argued, cannot afford a submarine gap.

This elevates submarines to a status they don’t deserve. It is only mildly reductionist to say that a submarine is merely a transportation device, a way to move weapons (torpedoes and missiles) and the sensors that support them (sonars, infrared cameras and more) closer to their targets.

There are other ways to do that. If the mission is to sink enemy ships, you can use aircraft, surface ships and even missile-armed trucks. If the mission is to hit a target on the enemy’s territory, you can use bombers or long-range missiles. Granted, submarines can do things that these other platforms cannot and Australia is better off with submarines than without them – but not at any cost. If we must have a submarine gap, then we can compensate with other capabilities.

The government also has the alliance to consider. It is one thing to upset the French, but the Americans present altogether higher stakes. The entire AUKUS initiative has deep roots in Australia’s traditional fear of great-power abandonment. But we overstate the extent to which the purchase of American equipment will compel them to continue defending us and we exaggerate the damage that will be done by backing out. France, Germany and Türkiye caused far more offence to Washington in 2002-03 when they actively worked against the Bush administration’s plans to invade Iraq. All remain members of NATO to this day.

Should the Liberal Party’s doubts grow stronger, though, it will create “permission” for the government to move in the same direction. The whole reason the Labor government finds itself in this position is that when AUKUS was announced, less than a year before the 2022 federal election, the then opposition spotted a political trap – an unpopular Morrison government was baiting the Labor Party to oppose the initiative so the Liberals could revive their electoral fortunes by engineering a “khaki election”. Labor refused to take the bait, endorsing AUKUS immediately. If doubts on the Liberal side grow stronger and they even begin to see AUKUS as a stick with which to beat the government, the Labor Party’s incentives will change.

This is a slow drip, however. For a circuit breaker, a force that could disrupt AUKUS in a matter of days rather than months or years, it can only be US President Trump. The government recognised Trump’s unpopularity in Australia from the beginning and benefited from it electorally in 2025 when the Dutton opposition flirted with MAGA-ism and paid the price. The 2025 Lowy Institute Poll showed a 20-point drop in Australians’ trust in the US to act responsibly in the world.

We see this anxiety reflected also in Marles’s recent speech to the Lowy Institute, in which he implicitly distanced his government from Trump by arguing that Labor has always been the party committed to Australian independence. Quite how that squares with the embrace of AUKUS and the agreement to station US forces in Western Australia and the Northern Territory was not explained.

Australia has escaped lightly in its dealings with Trump so far. Indeed, last October’s Trump–Albanese White House meeting was a political triumph for the government. But so mercurial is this US administration that the relationship could change in an instant. Canada is the cautionary tale here and it is notable that Prime Minister Mark Carney has responded to Trump’s provocations by insisting that Canada should become less dependent on American weapons “so we are never hostage to the decisions of others when it comes to our security”.

In truth, that’s not a realistic ambition for Canada, which is bound to the US by geography. Australia faces no such physical constraints – only the psychological one of refusing to believe we can face a difficult regional security environment on our own.
